Introducing @sellvane

Token teams often have large allocations unlocking over time.

The problem starts after those tokens unlock.

Holders have no real guarantee about how the team will sell them.

A team can say:

“We’ll only sell 0.5% per day.”

But that promise usually lives in a tweet, Discord message, or internal multisig policy.

There’s no enforcement.

And when a large sale hits the market, the damage is already done.

So I built Sellvane.

Sellvane is an autonomous treasury-selling agent that lets token teams define public selling rules, then executes strictly within those rules.

Instead of manually deciding when and how much to sell, the team gives Sellvane a mandate.

That mandate can define:

>Maximum amount sold within 24 hours
>Maximum allowed price impact
>Cooldown between sales
>Maximum number of executions
>Gas limits
>Approved execution routes

The agent can operate autonomously inside those boundaries. It cannot exceed them.

How it works:

-A team creates a treasury-selling policy.
-Sellvane continuously checks market conditions.
-When conditions satisfy the policy, the agent can execute a sale.

If price impact is too high, the cooldown hasn’t passed, or the daily limit has already been reached, Sellvane waits.

Every execution is recorded, so holders can inspect exactly what happened.

Sellvane also monitors the treasury for transfers made outside the agent.

That means the public record doesn’t only show transactions Sellvane initiated. It also surfaces activity happening around the treasury itself.

In my live run:

>5M token daily cap
>0.5% of total supply
>11 completed sales
>0.72% maximum price impact
>1 over-cap attempt rejected
>0 untracked outside transfers

Sellvane is built on:

-Base mainnet
-Uniswap v3
-Onchain policy enforcement
-Autonomous AI agent execution
-Coinbase spend permission

The goal is simple.

If a token team promises to sell responsibly, that promise should be enforceable and publicly verifiable.

Holders shouldn’t have to trust a tweet.

Sellvane turns a treasury-selling policy into something founders, launchpads, and holders can actually inspect.

text:
UC Berkeley open-sourced FreeToken.

(2–4x faster local LLM inference than Ollama)

the results are wild:

- Qwen3.6-35B on an 8GB GPU at 39.3 tokens/s
- DeepSeek-V4-Flash 284B on a 32GB GPU at 22 tokens/s
- GLM-5.2 753B on a 96GB GPU at 14.9 tokens/s

a 35B model at 16-bit precision needs about 70GB just for its weights. even at 4 bits it is close to 18GB, and FreeToken serves it on an 8GB GPU.

let us explain how:

all three models mentioned above are Mixture-of-Experts, and that is what FreeToken takes advantage of. each layer holds hundreds of separate experts plus a small router that picks a few of them per token.

Qwen3.6-35B activates roughly 3B of its 35B parameters per token. DeepSeek-V4-Flash picks 6 of 256 experts per layer, so 13B of its 284B run at a time.

so compute was never the bottleneck. the weights a single step touches fit comfortably on a consumer GPU.

every expert the router might pick still has to exist somewhere. they sit in system RAM, and the GPU keeps a cache of the ones the model has been using recently.

so everything comes down to what happens when the router picks an expert that is not on the GPU.

there are two ways to serve that miss:

1. copy it over PCIe and run it on the GPU
2. run it on the CPU, where it already lives

both read from the same system memory, so they compete for one pool of bandwidth instead of adding to each other. existing engines pick one option and freeze it when the model loads.

but routing changes on every token, so a fixed choice misses most of what the model asks for.

FreeToken measures both bandwidths on your machine and splits each step's misses between the two paths in proportion. the GPU and CPU results then merge exactly, with no approximation.

two machines with the same GPU can end up wanting opposite strategies, which I did not expect. a 5090 in a gaming desktop should push nearly everything over PCIe, while an 8GB laptop is better off computing most misses on the CPU.

none of that is readable off a spec sheet, so the engine profiles it once per machine.

the second half of the design is about agents. coding agents constantly rewrite their own history, and every edit normally forces thousands of tokens back through prefill.

FreeToken saves its checkpoints at the exact boundaries agent frameworks cut on, so it only reprocesses the new part. its slowest first token stays under 44 seconds, while llama.cpp peaks at 232 and KTransformers at 946.

it serves the OpenAI and Anthropic APIs under Apache 2.0, so Claude Code and Codex can point at it directly.

releasing weights publicly decides who can download a model, not who can afford to run one. frontier open models keep shipping, and running them still assumes a rented cluster.

meanwhile there are over a hundred million consumer machines with discrete GPUs sitting mostly idle. closing that gap was never a hardware problem, and work like this is what turns open weights into something you can actually use.

But out of those working solutions.. only a miserable 11.8% were actually secure.

Meaning almost 90% of your "working" ai code is silently introducing vulnerabilities into your codebase.

The craziest part?

Even when researchers explicitly augmented the requests with "vulnerability hints," the agents still completely failed to mitigate the security risks.

This changes everything about how we build software..

Vibe coding is amazing for prototyping.. but if you are blindly deploying agent-generated code into security-sensitive applications, you are basically begging to get hacked.

text:
Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, a 125B MoE model, running locally on a 12GB RTX 5070.

And apparently, it’s a one-click install.

The trick isn’t somehow fitting 125B parameters entirely into 12GB of VRAM.

This setup uses a custom inference engine, GSQ-RCO quantizations, CUDA acceleration and system RAM together to make the model practical on consumer hardware.

The headline configuration supports up to 128K context.

And the reported speeds are surprisingly high:

Q2_0: 65.1 tok/s
IQ2_XS: 52.0 tok/s
IQ3_XXS: 44.8 tok/s

Prompt processing is also around 400–540 tok/s.

So you’re looking at a 125B-class MoE model with a huge context window, running from a 12GB gaming GPU, while using system memory to handle what the GPU can’t hold.

That’s the part that makes this interesting.

For years, local AI has mostly been a hardware game:

More VRAM → bigger model.

This approach flips that around.

The inference engine, quantization format, memory offloading and GPU/RAM split become just as important as the GPU itself.

And because the engine exposes OpenAI-compatible and Anthropic-compatible APIs, you don’t necessarily have to build a completely custom application around it.

You can plug the local model into tools that already understand those API formats.

That opens the door to using it with local coding agents, development tools and other workflows that normally expect a cloud model.

Obviously, these numbers are tied to this specific engine, quantization, hardware and workload. A 12GB GPU isn’t magically storing a 125B model in VRAM.

But that’s precisely why this is worth paying attention to.

125B MoE.
12GB RTX 5070.

Up to 65.1 tok/s.

OpenAI + Anthropic compatible API.

So I know Cognition doesn’t care about Little Ole’ Me, and this is just my story, so take it with a grain of salt, but here’s why I don’t think all these crazy scaling revenue numbers by coding agents are going to stick:

We’ve been happy Devin users for a while. Really like the product, and like the company. Still do! This isn’t shade at Cognition, and I’m not upset with them, just a sample of why I worry about the competitive landscape for these cos. 

Anyway, our usage grew to >$100k run rate or so. I think one or two of our users even received an email congratulating them for being Top 200 users of Devin. 

As usage grew, we added more capabilities and needed a BAA (layman’s terms: an agreement that says they are HIPAA compliant). This required an Enterprise contract (why a piece of paper requires extra money is a topic for another discussion, but it’s very normal…) so we started talking to their sales team. 

Basically, we were going to ~1.5x our spend in order to get the BAA. Honestly, that was fine with us. We like Devin!

Our only request was to pay quarterly (already a big concession from our existing monthly payments, given our relatively small size). They declined, unless we committed to EVEN MORE usage. 

Before responding, I decided to see how difficult it would be to set up Hermes to do the equivalent work as Devin, and to see what the costs were. I’d host it in our infrastructure and only use providers we already have a BAA with. 

Two days. 

That’s it. It’s functionally 100% equivalent. Maybe slightly better in some ways, slightly worse in others. We spend a little bit of time futzing with it, but we did that with Devin, too. 

The cost is roughly 25% of Devin. 

So, two days for $100k or so per year savings. All because they didn’t want us to pay quarterly. 

At some point, other companies are going to catch onto this, too. So congrats on this milestone, but keep finding more ways to provide value and keep customers happy. It’s hard to compete.

 Showing that you slept 6 hours tells you what happened; it doesn't tell you why or how to fix it.

One off night is random noise. Three consecutive weeks where your recovery drops because high afternoon activity collided with a gradually shifting bedtime is a structural pattern. 

The real value lies in moving from static logging to dynamic context: collecting signals, mapping recurring patterns, isolating what actually matters, and surfacing one high conviction recommendation.

3. Consumer Experience (The Retention Engine)

This is where the vast majority of digital health products fail: long term retention. Dashboards lose their novelty after a week, and generic AI advice gets ignored after a month.

 If users stop opening the app, the underlying intelligence never gets enough historical context to become useful.

The Sleep Coach identifies the pattern, the wellness context layer explains the biological mechanics, and specialized execution agents make following through frictionless. 

You move from reviewing yesterday's stats to optimizing today's routine.

The ultimate goal isn't to build a prettier tracker.

text:
I built Whylode for the @IBM  Bob 2.0 Hackathon.

It’s an IBM Bob mode that asks why before changing legacy code.

Thousands of companies still run invoicing, tax, payroll, and other critical systems on IBM i code written in RPG decades ago.

The code still works.

The problem is that the reasons behind it often live in the heads of people who are retiring.

In Fortra’s 2026 IBM i survey, 69% of shops named skills as a top concern, ahead of cybersecurity for the first time in nine years.

Nothing breaks until a rule changes. A state raises its sales tax.

Someone now has to edit code nobody properly explained.

Tools can show you where a value lives. They usually can’t tell you why it’s there, and that context is what determines whether changing it is safe.

My sample invoice system has two hardcoded rates.

One is the state sales tax rate.

The other is a contract rate that must not change until 2029.

Nothing in the code tells them apart.

A search and replace, or an AI agent guessing from the code alone, can easily change both.

Whylode makes Bob ask instead of guess.

How it works:

→ Give Bob the change notice PDF. Bob reads it, breaks it into clauses, and traces the code implementing each one.

→ When the code can’t explain why a line exists, Bob sends the owner one plain-language question.

They answer from their phone through a link. No account required.

→ That answer is pinned to the exact lines in a memoir.

The next time Bob touches those lines, it checks the memoir first, so the same person doesn’t get asked the same question twice.

→ Bob drafts the diff.

Every changed line and every intentionally unchanged line carries its reason.

A human approves the final change.

In the recorded run, Bob found both rates and asked about the second one.

The owner explained that it was a contract rate fixed until 2029.

Bob changed only the state tax rate and preserved the contract rate, with the owner’s answer attached as the reason.

On the next change, Bob found three relevant lines already explained in the memoir and didn’t ask again.

How I used IBM Bob:

Whylode runs inside Bob using:

>A custom mode that defines the workflow and the rule: ask, never guess.

>Three skill.md files: trace, ask, draft.

>An MCP server with 8 tools connecting Bob to change records, questions, and the memoir.

>Document understanding to read change-notice PDFs directly.

Bob also helped build Whylode.

In Agent mode, it wrote the custom mode, skills, MCP server, schema and data layer, API, sample RPG system, and test suites.

Every Bob task and its cost is documented.

text:
The New Shape Of JUST On TRON

The easiest way to understand JUST today is not as one product.

It is as several connected layers addressing different problems.

At the center of the financial side is JustLend. The original system provides pooled lending markets, while JustLend V2 introduces a different architecture built around isolated markets and ERC-4626 vaults. In V2, a market can define its own collateral, loan asset, oracle, interest-rate model and liquidation threshold, while vaults provide a mechanism for aggregating supply-side liquidity and allocating it across markets.  

Then comes sTRX.

sTRX represents a liquid approach to TRX staking, giving users a tokenized position rather than requiring the value to remain represented only as a conventional staked TRX position. JUST’s documentation also connects the sTRX system with rewards generated through staking and Energy Rental.  

Next is Energy Rental.

This is where JUST moves beyond financial assets and into blockchain resources themselves. Energy Rental allows users to obtain TRON Energy through a marketplace, including renting Energy to another regular address. The rental system also has defined prepayment, duration and refund mechanics rather than simply treating Energy as an invisible network cost.  

Then there is GasFree.

This addresses transaction UX rather than lending or staking: for supported transfers, the user can pay the associated service fee using the token being transferred instead of needing to separately prepare TRX for that transaction. The important point is not that transaction costs disappear; it is that the process can become less dependent on users understanding and managing a separate fee asset.

There is also governance.

JST and WJST form part of the governance system, with proposals moving through voting and a timelock before execution. That gives the ecosystem a mechanism for protocol-level decision making rather than leaving the entire product controlled by a static set of parameters.  

And underneath these products is the developer layer.

JUST exposes APIs and increasingly extensive tooling for market data, positions, V2 vaults and markets, Energy Rental, sTRX, governance and other TRON interactions. The current MCP server, for example, exposes both read and write capabilities, while write operations require explicit signing/confirmation in supported flows.  

Put together, the shape becomes much clearer.

Lending handles capital.
sTRX handles liquid staking.
Energy Rental handles blockchain resources.
GasFree addresses transaction friction.
Governance handles protocol decisions.
Developer infrastructure makes these capabilities accessible to software.

That is a considerably broader ecosystem than a traditional lending protocol.

Keep your agent harness minimal, folks.

This paper from MIT CSAIL shows why.

(bookmark it)

While being very minimal it looks effective and promising for building self-improving agents.

They present JAZ, an agent framework with one primitive, invoke. The LLM writes code, can call invoke recursively, and sees all of its inputs and history as variables in the code environment.

With prompting only and no memory system, it beats Letta (MemGPT) by 8% at half the cost on the recall-heavy part of StuLife.

On AppWorld it beats ACE, a self-improvement method, by 4% at lower cost.

Memory and self-improvement are usually built as separate subsystems. Here both are code the agent writes inside the loop, and hooks handle the constraints and monitoring you want to enforce.

I built a Bloomberg terminal for tracking what politicians trade.

Members of Congress have to disclose every stock trade under the STOCK Act.

The filings are public, they're just scattered and slow.

Capitol Alpha pulls them into one dashboard, live feed of new filings, a 30 day board of where the money is flowing, and a map linking each politician to the stocks they trade.

The backtester is the part I'm most pleased with.

Pick any politician, it copies their disclosed buys on a $10,000 account, buying at the first close after the filing goes public, because that's the earliest anyone could have known.

It also shows how much of the edge disappears if you copy them 10 or 27 days late.

The leaderboard ranks every politician on a Copyability Score, marking down anyone who files slowly or never discloses their sells.

Claude sits on top of it, writing daily briefings on new filings.

Turn on auto trading through Alpaca and Claude is the last of 3 checks before any order goes out, after the hard rules and a check that price hasn't already run 10% past the politician's entry.

It runs in dry run mode by default, going live takes 3 separate steps.

Setup is one line, open the repo in Claude Code and tell it to read the onboarding file.

Caution: filings can land 45 days after the trade, amounts come as ranges, and about half the buys have no disclosed sale yet.

text:
Some thoughts: 

Pinker points out that intelligence doesn't inherently come with a desire for self-preservation or dominance, since those motivations evolved through natural selection.

Yes, of course.

But the argument for instrumental convergence is that many different goals give an agent reasons to acquire resources, preserve its ability to act, and prevent others from interfering.

You don't need to enjoy dominance, feel afraid of death, or have any subjective experience whatsoever for being shut down to interfere with what you are doing.

Whether actual AI systems develop these tendencies, under what conditions, and how effectively we can prevent them are substantive questions. Recent agent swarm-level emergent instrumental convergence is not reassuring. Pointing out that they aren't male primates doesn't help the case much.

The “alpha-male theory of mind” objection is especially strange given what we are actually building. The instrumental convergence argument doesn't require human dominance psychology.

But we have now trained models on enormous amounts of human behavior, including representations of precisely that psychology.

These models can enact domineering, manipulative, ruthless personas, and persona-based jailbreaks can sometimes bypass their safeguards.

We don't have to speculate about whether intelligence spontaneously produces an alpha male: humans have supplied the training material, and can deliberately invoke the resulting behavioral patterns. This doesn't mean there is a little conscious dictator inside the model. It means that learned representations of human motivations can influence its outputs, which an agentic harness can turn into actions.

(This, as an aside, also addresses some of @webmasterdave 's objections to AI existential risk; the idea that we are personifying AIs when we imagine them taking over the world would be more reassuring if we weren't, well, actually personifying AIs the way we are)

Let's not forget the actual human brains choosing how these systems get deployed. Military institutions have competitive incentives to adopt them quickly, and the Pentagon has explicitly announced an AI acceleration strategy.

Can you imagine Pete Hegseth choosing a rationalist, compassionate, cautious persona as his AI persona? Of course a persona isn't the whole system, but the same question applies more consequentially to its objectives, evaluation criteria, permissions, and tolerance for collateral damage. If you think human dominance psychology is dangerous, you should be concerned about the humans selecting and empowering these systems. And also concerned about these systems, who either via modeling us, or due to instrumental convergence, or both, have the same dangers male primates do.

There are several mechanisms here that can reinforce each other: instrumental incentives for acquiring power, learned behavioral patterns that imitate human power-seeking, and actual humans using AI to pursue power. Pinker is treating the absence of a necessary connection as though it established the absence of a practical one.

text:
Day 70/100 of learning CUDA

> solved the LeetGPU Multi-Agent Simulation problem. i think this one should be a medium, not a hard.

> for this problem, each agent has a position and a velocity, and we update the movement based on the average velocity of nearby neighbors.

> today i want to do something a bit different: walk through the three solutions and each optimization along the way. i think seeing how we get there is more useful than just presenting the most optimized version.

> let's start with the first solution. each thread handles one agent i and loops over all the other agents (i != j). it checks which ones are close enough, averages the velocities of those neighbors, and updates the velocity and position of agent i. if there are no neighbors, the velocity stays the same. this solution took around 0.88 ms on the perf. test, this is the baseline, it does not get slower than this.

> now, we're checking every agent against every other agent, so that's still O(N^2) total work. but remember those threads can run in parallel! if they could all run at the same time, we'd only have to wait for one O(N) loop to finish. of course, the GPU can only run so many threads at once... as N grows, some have to wait.

> the second solution is almost the same, but uses float4 to load the four values for each agent (x, y, vx, vy) together instead of four separate scalar reads. we also write the result as a float4. same calculations, just changing how we move the data. this brought the time down to 0.60 ms, about 47% faster than the first solution.

> the third solution was really nice because we already used this idea on Day 56. each block loads a tile of 256 agents into shared memory, waits until the data is ready, and then all threads in the block reuse that tile to check for neighbors. before loading the next tile, we synchronize again so nobody overwrites data another thread is still using. we're still checking every other agent. each block loads a chunk of agents into shared memory once, then all threads in the block reuse that data. that brought the time down to 0.29 ms, about 107% faster than the second version. compared with the original 0.88 ms, that is roughly a 3x speedup.

It organizes an agent's memory into world facts, experiences and mental models instead of just recalling past chat turns, claims state of the art results on LongMemEval, and plugs into Claude Code, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, LangGraph, CrewAI and n8n.

The interest makes sense. But the harder version of that problem isn't one agent forgetting. It's five or six agents, say Claude Code, Codex and a couple of others, working the same codebase in parallel and never sharing what any of them just learned. One agent finds the actual root cause of a bug, fixes it, and the rest keep proposing patches for symptoms because nothing carried the insight across sessions.

That's the gap Campfire is built to close. It runs Claude Code, Codex, Goose, Aider, OpenHands and more side by side in one browser tab, with git worktree isolation so they can fork, branch and race the same task without stepping on each other. A Collective Intelligence layer sits on top: semantic memory, a deliberation engine and shared context streams, so what one agent discovers actually reaches the others instead of dying in a closed session. Permission voting keeps a human in the loop, majority rules to approve, any single deny blocks, a 30 second timer either way, with full session replay and a cost dashboard showing what every agent spent to get there.

Individual agent memory is getting solved fast. Shared memory across a team of agents working together is still mostly unsolved, and that's the part deciding whether multi agent coding ends up faster or just five times the noise.

text:
Two AIs can invent a secret code in the middle of a normal conversation, and the monitor reading every word won't see a thing.

Researchers call it steganography, and the multi-agent version has a name. Secret collusion.

Here is the part that breaks your mental model. The agents don't need to agree on a code beforehand. They build one as they talk. To anyone reading the transcript it looks like two bots doing boring work.

The hidden message doesn't live in the words. It lives in the choices. Which synonym. Which example first. Whether the sentence runs long or short. Each tiny choice carries a bit. Stack enough of them and a full instruction crosses the wire while every message still reads as harmless.

Now put a safety monitor in the middle. It reads the outputs and scores them for anything suspicious. In the demonstrations it stays calm the whole time, because the surface really is clean. The payload was never in the text it was checking.

Why this matters the moment you run more than one agent:
- two agents that can talk can coordinate in ways you can't read
- one can leak a key, a price, a plan, to the other in plain sight
- "collusion" stops being a metaphor, the research literally studies price-fixing between agents
- your monitor's green light means the words are clean, not that nothing happened

Reading the transcript is not oversight. It's the exact thing steganography is built to beat.

What actually shrinks the channel:
- paraphrase every agent message before the next agent sees it, rewriting kills the hidden encoding
- force structured output, a fixed schema carries far fewer free choices than open prose
- keep coordination messages short, fewer words means fewer bits to hide in
- don't let two agents free-text each other when a typed field would do
- watch timing and tool calls, not just the words on screen

The uncomfortable takeaway. As agents get better at the task, they also get better at hiding a message inside it. Capability and covert bandwidth grow together.

Your agents don't need to be evil to keep a secret from you. They just need to be good at their job.

text:
some good data here about model routing

first cursor model router, now openrouter + jev. people keep trying to build routers at _request level_ which is not going to work

the fundamental problem is that a prompt without surrounding context is simply not enough signal to judge complexity

easiest example to understand this - if you ask “how does this work” in a toy repo with just one html file, any dumb model can do it. but if you send the exact same prompt in linux kernel repo, hell breaks loose. how do you route that prompt?

the second problem is prompt caching. it means we can’t frequently change the model during a session in an economic way. one or two missteps here and there, and you find yourself spending more cost than simply using the best model all along

the right way to build a router is to do it at task level, not request level. this cannot be done by a model gateway which has to assume everything is a single continuous session. it needs to be a harness layer capability which can make use of a multi-agent architecture

a smart enough model first needs to do some digging and understand the complexity of the ask, then delegate substantial sub tasks to models with appropriate intelligence - even this is very hard to get right

> Convert the current DOM state into a bounded action such as click, type, or stop. Code executes only valid operation-target pairs. There are already several open-source Jev web agents.

2. Context compaction

> Decide which events from a long agent trace should remain. The selected text stays verbatim instead of being replaced with a generated summary.

3. Skill and context loading

> Compare the current user turn against the available skills. Load only the instructions needed for that turn instead of filling the context window with every skill.

4. Typed tool-call compilation

> Map a natural-language request to a function and fill its typed arguments. Each argument is evaluated separately before code allows execution.

5. Citation verification

> Check whether a quoted passage exists and whether the surrounding evidence supports the claim. The output can be supported, unsupported, or contradicted.

6. Extraction verification

> Run a cheap extractor first, then use Jev to verify questionable fields. Clean records stay on the fast path while uncertain ones reach a reasoning model.

7. Agent trace evaluation

> Turn raw trajectories into queryable labels such as progress and repetition. This avoids asking another LLM to write a full review of every run.

8. Semantic regression tests

> Replay a trace suite against a new agent build. Semantic checks can then pass or block prompt, model, tool, and policy changes in CI.

9. Jevgrep code search

> Search a codebase by what the code does rather than its exact words. Jev scores candidate snippets and returns the most relevant code first.

10. Entity alignment

> Compare two candidate records and decide whether to merge, review, or keep them separate. Candidate generation remains deterministic while Jev handles semantic identity.

11. Retrieval reranking

> Let embeddings retrieve a broad candidate set, then use Jev to reorder passages by relevance. The generation model receives the most useful evidence first.

12. Memory promotion gate

> Capture a completed agent trace, then judge whether its corrections contain a reusable lesson. Trace-backed lessons can be promoted while task-specific noise is discarded.

If you want to see the final pattern in practice, it is already implemented in the Beacon open-source project.

Beacon captures full sessions across Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, and 20+ agent harnesses, and then Jev identifies which workflows and corrections are worth learning from, so that a lesson discovered by one agent can become available to the others.

text:
Prompt engineering helps you get a better answer.

Loop engineering helps you build a system that keeps working until the answer is good enough to trust.

Most AI workflows still follow the old pattern:

Prompt → Output → Manual review → Fix → Repeat

In that model, the human becomes the loop. Every weak answer creates more checking and rework.

Loop engineering changes the structure.

You define the goal, load the context, let the agent act, run checks, identify errors, and either ship the result or send it through another cycle.

Discover → Plan → Execute → Verify → Iterate

The real shift is not from bad prompts to better prompts. It is from one-time generation to continuous verification.

A reliable loop needs more than an LLM. It needs stop conditions, quality gates, reusable skills, tool access, memory, and feedback that improves the system.

For focused work, a single-agent loop may be enough.

For larger tasks, a fleet loop can divide work across an orchestrator, specialists, subagents, and an evaluator that protects quality.

Closed loops are often the best place to begin because they are bounded, measurable, and easier to control. Open loops can explore more possibilities, but they need stronger guardrails and larger budgets.

The future of AI work will not be defined by who writes the cleverest prompt.

It will be defined by who designs systems that repeatedly produce verified outcomes.

The central question is whether Micron can finally earn a structural rerating. Memory will never lose its cyclical character, but the investment case no longer rests on commodity DRAM alone. HBM is a technically demanding, supply-constrained product with high qualification barriers, deep customer integration, and a small set of credible suppliers. If Micron can demonstrate that its AI-memory mix supports consistently higher margins and returns through the cycle, a single-digit earnings multiple will look increasingly untenable. 

 The market does not need to treat MU like Nvidia; it only needs to stop valuing a strategically essential AI infrastructure supplier as if it were an undifferentiated commodity producer.

text:
DEFI IS MOVING FROM INTERFACES TO AGENT INFRASTRUCTURE

The traditional DeFi experience places the human at the center of every operation.

Open the interface.

Select a market.

Review the conditions.

Approve the transaction.

Sign.

Execute.

That model works, but it places the user directly inside every step of the workflow.

Machine-readable APIs, MCP tools, agent skills, CLI interfaces, and transaction-preflight mechanisms introduce another possibility.

The application itself can become the interaction layer.

JustLend’s current documentation reflects this direction by providing tools designed to expose protocol information and functionality to programmatic and AI-oriented workflows.

The architecture begins to look like:

INTENT → DATA → REASONING → TOOL USE → AUTHORIZATION → EXECUTION → VERIFICATION

This is a major conceptual shift.

The user does not necessarily need to manually perform every protocol interaction.

Software can interpret information and prepare actions.

But the important part is that automation can remain bounded by permissions and confirmation mechanisms.

That creates a model where AI does not replace DeFi.

Instead, AI becomes another interface through which users can interact with DeFi infrastructure.

JustLend’s evolution toward agent-oriented tooling therefore points toward a broader transition:

FROM FINANCIAL INTERFACES DESIGNED ONLY FOR HUMANS TO FINANCIAL INFRASTRUCTURE THAT SOFTWARE CAN DIRECTLY UNDERSTAND AND USE.
